findings.trigger_condition: Input edges contain N unhashable node values (lists, dicts, or custom objects with __hash__=None). With N unhashable nodes forming a chain or star graph, every node lookup after the first performs a linear scan over all previously registered unhashable AND hashable nodes, making total processing time O(N^2).
findings.root_cause: The `_id_of` function's unhashable path (lines 63-75) performs two linear scans: `for existing_id in unhashable_ids` (line 64) and `for existing_id in hashable_ids` (line 68). Each new unhashable node must be compared against all U existing unhashable nodes and all H existing hashable nodes. With N nodes this is O(N) per registration, giving O(N^2) total time for N edges. The code comment at line 59-60 acknowledges no constant-time lookup exists for unhashable values, but the implementation also lacks an identity-based fast path (e.g., `id(value) -> node_id` dict) that would make repeated appearances of the same object O(1) instead of O(N).
findings.impact: Quadratic time complexity makes the function unsuitable for large inputs with unhashable nodes. Benchmarked: N=200 takes 0.003s, N=400 takes 0.010s (~3.7x), N=800 takes 0.040s (~3.9x), N=1600 takes 0.155s (~3.9x) — confirming O(N^2) scaling. At N=10000 unhashable nodes this would take ~6 seconds; at N=50000 it would take minutes. By contrast, all-hashable inputs process 100000 nodes in 0.19s (linear).
findings.suggested_validation: Run with edges containing N unhashable nodes (e.g., lists) in a chain or star topology. Measure wall-clock time for N=200,400,800,1600 and verify time ratio approaches 4x per doubling (quadratic). Compare against all-hashable inputs of the same size to confirm the O(N^2) vs O(N) gap.

findings.trigger_condition: When ANY unhashable nodes are registered, EVERY subsequent hashable value lookup performs an unconditional O(U) linear scan over all unhashable_ids to check for cross-type equality, even when no cross-type equality relationship can exist. For H hashable lookups with U unhashable nodes present, this adds O(H*U) overhead.
findings.root_cause: Lines 83-87 unconditionally iterate over the entire `unhashable_ids` list for every hashable value lookup: `for existing_id in unhashable_ids: if _same_node(...)`. This scan exists solely to handle the rare edge case where a hashable Python object compares equal to an unhashable one (e.g., a custom class with __eq__ matching tuples but no __hash__). In the common case where no such cross-type equality exists, this scan is pure overhead with O(U) cost per hashable lookup and no early-exit optimization.
findings.impact: A single unhashable node degrades all subsequent hashable lookups from O(1) to O(U). Benchmarked: with U=4000 unhashable nodes, just 2 additional hashable node lookups take 0.50s. With U=2000 they take 0.13s. For workloads mixing a moderate number of unhashable nodes with many hashable edges, the cross-type scan dominates runtime even though cross-type equality almost never applies.
findings.suggested_validation: Register U unhashable nodes first, then add a single edge with two hashable nodes. Measure total time for U=1000,2000,4000 and confirm linear growth in U even though only 2 hashable lookups occur. Verify that removing lines 83-87 (or guarding them behind a flag set only when cross-type equality is actually detected) eliminates this overhead while passing cross-type equality tests.
